name: Satchinathar Temple, Avalivanallur
deity: Shiva as Satchinathar (the witness lord), with the goddess Soundaranayaki
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam and a Pancha Aranya Sthalam
summary: Avalivanallur, near Kumbakonam, honours Shiva as Satchinathar — the lord who himself stood witness. By tradition a devout priest, returning from Kashi, could not recognise his sickness-worn wife beside her healthy sister, and the lord appeared to testify to the truth, taking the name Satchinathar, 'Satchi' meaning witness. A Paadal Petra Sthalam sung by Sambandar and Sundarar, it is also one of the Pancha Aranya Sthalams, the five forest temples near Kumbakonam, set once amid a grove of trumpet-flower trees.

sections.history: Avalivanallur is an ancient Shaiva village near Kumbakonam, hymned in the seventh-century Tevaram by Sambandar and Sundarar and counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams. It belongs also to the Pancha Aranya Sthalams — the five 'forest' temples near Kumbakonam, this one once set in the Pathiri Vanam, a forest of trumpet-flower trees. The stone temple is of the Chola period with later additions; its enduring renown is for the tender legend that gives the lord his name.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Dravidian plan with a gopuram, prakara and the sanctum of Satchinathar, with the goddess Soundaranayaki in her own shrine. As one of the Pancha Aranya temples, it shares in a circuit of five forest shrines that pilgrims visit together. The trumpet-flower tree of its old forest setting is remembered as the sthala vriksham, linking the quiet village temple to its wooded past.
sections.legends: The defining legend explains the name Satchinathar, the witness lord. A devout priest married and then set out on pilgrimage to Kashi. In his absence his wife fell ill, and her sister came to nurse her; when the priest returned he found two women — one wasted by sickness, the other healthy and resembling his wife — and could not tell which was his own. The lord himself then appeared as witness to affirm the wife's word, and from this act of divine testimony takes the name Satchinathar. The story has made the temple a place associated with truth, trust and the vindication of the faithful.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva festival calendar — Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham, the Margazhi season and the annual Brahmotsavam. Pilgrims undertaking the Pancha Aranya circuit of the five forest temples include Avalivanallur among their stops, so the temple shares in that group pilgrimage as well as its own local observances.
sections.experience: Avalivanallur offers the pilgrim a tender, human story at the heart of its worship — a god who stood as witness for a wronged and unrecognised wife. The darshan of Satchinathar carries this sense of a lord who vindicates the truthful, and completing the Pancha Aranya circuit gives the visit the added depth of a wider forest pilgrimage.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Avalivanallur is in Tiruvarur district near Kumbakonam, roughly 15 km away; Kumbakonam is the nearest rail head and town, with local buses and taxis to the village.
